abstract: Stanford Digital Economy Lab Research Note #1: AI Economic Indicators June 2026 Update (Erik Brynjolfsson, director). Establishes three linked, high-frequency dashboards to track AI's economic impact: (1) the Canaries Dashboard, run in partnership with ADP Research, tracking employment by age and AI exposure across a 5-year balanced ADP payroll sample of ~25,000 firms and 4.6M workers; (2) the Takeoff Tracker, monitoring 12 aggregate US indicators of AI-driven economic 'takeoff'; and (3) the Adoption Monitor, synthesizing individual and firm adoption surveys. The overarching message: aggregate employment differences by AI exposure are modest, but early-career workers (ages 22-25) in the most-exposed occupations are contracting sharply; there is no decisive evidence of macroeconomic takeoff yet; and adoption is widespread and US-led.
keyFindings: Canaries (all ages): most-AI-exposed occupations growing 1.1%/yr vs 2.0%/yr for least-exposed since ChatGPT — modest divergence
Canaries (early career 22-25, 7.4% of sample): most-exposed occupations contracting 3.8%/yr vs +2.0%/yr for least-exposed — pronounced divergence, has intensified in 9 months since original paper
Automation ratio (Anthropic Economic Index) correlates with employment declines; augmentation ratio does NOT — 'the character of AI usage could shape the labor market effects'
Specific occupations: early-career software developers and customer-service reps show substantial declines; home health aides (less-exposed) show early-career growth
Sample: 5-year balanced ADP panel, 25,000 firms, 4.6M workers as of Nov 2022, 730+ occupations; most-exposed quintile = 38.3% of employment, least-exposed = 6.4%
Takeoff Tracker (12 indicators as of May 2026): 7 no evidence, 3 mild evidence, 2 strong evidence — 'no decisive evidence of takeoff'
Takeoff — Capital share: STRONG evidence (persistent upward trend consistent with capital substituting for labor)
Takeoff — Total factor productivity growth: NEUTRAL (no break from recent levels)
Takeoff — Information-processing equipment share of private nonresidential equipment: MILD evidence (recovering to early-2000s levels)

Adoption Monitor: individual work-adoption generally trending up but some recent workplace surveys show reversal; firm adoption widespread and US-led; robotics and autonomous vehicles show largest current-vs-expected gaps

Positions the research amid an active debate — cites Hosseini-Maasoum & Lichtinger (replicating), Humlum-Vestergaard (Denmark, similar pattern but firm-encouragement unrelated), Lambert-Schindler (remote-work confound), Yale Budget Lab and Eckhardt-Goldschlag (no aggregate effect), Johnston-Makridis (sector-level INCREASES), Tucker (early-career hiring declines that may predate ChatGPT)
methodology: Three complementary dashboards. Canaries: 5-year balanced sample of firms using ADP payroll services (25,000 firms, 4.6M workers matched to occupation, 730+ occupations aggregated from 6-digit SOC), applies Eloundou et al. (2024) GPT-exposure scores, tracks employment indices within age-x-exposure cells since Nov 2022. Uses Anthropic Economic Index (Massenkoff et al. 2026) to distinguish automation vs augmentation usage patterns. Takeoff Tracker: 12 aggregate US macro indicators (capital share, TFP growth, IP equipment share, and 9 others), each classified as no/mild/strong evidence of takeoff using pre-registered rules. Adoption Monitor: synthesis of individual-survey and firm-survey sources including Bick/Blandin/Deming, Gallup, Pew, Hartley et al., and Yotzov et al.
qualifiers: Canaries sample does not represent the entire US labor market — firm-composition differs from QCEW; sample is balanced (excludes firms that enter/exit) so does not capture inter-firm reallocation or entry/exit dynamics. Occupation-level analysis requires successful ADP occupation coding. Employment index for early-career workers (7.4% of sample) is a leading indicator, not a headline unemployment figure. Takeoff Tracker classifications depend on pre-registered thresholds; a 'no evidence' reading does not preclude eventual takeoff. Exposure scores from Eloundou et al. measure task-level LLM potential, not adoption. Future work will incorporate the AI Jobs Transition Framework (Richmond 2026) to account for demand elasticity — currently unaddressed in the exposure-only view.
